Best meditation apps of 2027 and how to choose the right one

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, you open the app store to look for a meditation app and find dozens of options promising calmer days, deeper sleep, less stress, and sharper focus.
  • It has been revealed that below, we cover three well-known meditation apps: Calm, Headspace, and Insight Timer.
  • Industry observers note that before we dive in, a quick note on where we’re coming from.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, you open the app store to look for a meditation app and find dozens of options promising calmer days, deeper sleep, less stress, and sharper focus. It’s hard to know where to start or which claims to believe.

It has been revealed that below, we cover three well-known meditation apps: Calm, Headspace, and Insight Timer. We've looked at what each one offers and named what we like about it, so you can decide which one to try.

Industry observers note that before we dive in, a quick note on where we’re coming from. We make Calm, and we love it. We hope you will too, but another option might suit you better.

According to recent reports, the best meditation app for you depends on what you’re looking for. To narrow it down, ask yourself these questions:.

Sources indicate that what do you want help with? Maybe it’s stress relief, better sleep, sharper focus, or a guided start as a beginner.

Industry observers note that how much variety do you need? Some people want an extensive library to explore, while others prefer a smaller collection built around a specific goal.

Sources indicate that how personal do you want it to feel? You might prefer an app that tailors recommendations to your mood and goals, or one that leaves the choosing to you.

What's your budget? Compare what the free and paid tiers include, since a generous free version may be all you need.

According to recent reports, calm is one of the most widely used meditation apps, and it also offers sleep content, music, gentle movement sessions, and more. People use Calm at night for sleep and during the day for stress.

Recent findings suggest that content library: The app features Sleep Stories, bedtime tales read by well-known voices, alongside daily meditation programs including the flagship Daily Calm. You'll also find breathwork exercises, mindful tools, soundscapes, intro courses, and longer programs on themes like anxiety and self-kindness.

Personalization: Calm’s Check-Ins let you log your mood, sleep, and gratitude, so you can spot patterns over time. You can set reminders and follow a series of sessions to build a routine.

Standout feature: For us, it's the sleep content. Sleep Stories are the first thing we’d recommend to a friend who’s struggling with sleep.

In a recent development, headspace is another widely-used meditation app, and it leans into teaching. Many sessions are organized into courses that walk you through a topic step by step.

Industry observers note that content library: The app features beginner courses and SOS meditations, short sessions for when stress spikes. It also has themed collections for focus and movement. For sleep, there are Sleepcasts.

Personalization: Headspace offers personalized recommendations and its AI companion, Ebb, lets you talk through how you’re feeling and suggests app content in response.

Standout feature: We like how Headspace gives beginners a clear path to follow, starting with its 10-session Basics course.

Insight Timer started as a meditation timer and grew into a large library of guided meditations, with plenty of free content and a paid tier called MemberPlus.

Content library: The app hosts a catalog of meditations, talks, and music tracks, plus a meditation timer for people who prefer to sit in silence.

Personalization: You can join teacher-led challenges to help you stay on track, and the streak feature tracks how many days in a row you’ve meditated.

Standout feature: We like how much the app offers for free. With so much available, you can try a range of teachers before paying for anything.

In a recent development, calm won’t be right for everyone, but here’s why we love it. (Keep in mind that this section is our point of view, not a neutral comparison.).

The daily meditations are a great place to start. There are three to choose from, and each has its own feel:.

The Daily Calm, with Tamara Levitt, leans toward gentle reflection.

The Daily Jay, with Jay Shetty, draws on psychology and timeless wisdom.

The Daily Trip, with Jeff Warren, suits curious meditators who like to experiment.

You may click with one voice more than the others, so it’s worth trying all three to find out whether you’re a Tamara, Jay, or Jeff person. (There’s a fourth daily too, the Daily Move, a short mindful movement session — a great way to get your body ready for the day.).

It has been revealed that we’ve also produced a lot of quick meditations over the past few years, all under five minutes. So even the busiest person, or the most skeptical first-timer, has something small to try.

Sleep is the other main reason we keep coming back. With our Sleep Stories and nighttime meditations, we’ve unlocked a delightful way to let go of the worries of the day, relax your mind and body, and allow yourself to fall (and stay) asleep easily and naturally. Our 500+ Sleep Stories include some of the world’s most celebrated and soothing voices, like Harry Styles, Cynthia Erivo, Idris Elba, Rosé, and Greta Lee. With plenty more to choose from, there’s always something fresh to help you wind down and drift off.

Recent findings suggest that then there’s how the app looks and feels. The visuals lean into calming nature—think misty forests, rain on a window, slow ocean waves—so opening the app itself sets the scene for calm. And if you just need to tune out the world for a while, our Rain on Leaves soundscape is a legit vibe.

The numbers back up the impact. More than 180 million people worldwide have downloaded Calm, and its content has been studied in peer-reviewed research. For example, in one randomized trial of 88 stressed college students, those who used Calm for eight weeks reported lower perceived stress than a wait-list group.

They may help, though the research is still young. An updated review of 45 randomized trials found improvements in anxiety and depression symptoms among people using mindfulness apps, compared with control groups. The effects were modest, and the authors note we still need larger, higher-quality studies to say how much apps help and for whom.

In a recent development, an app also isn’t a substitute for professional care. If you’re struggling with your mental health, it’s worth talking to a doctor, who can help you find the right support.

Related read: The science behind Calm: 27 studies and surveys.

According to recent reports, yes, though how much is free varies a lot. Calm and Headspace each offer a limited selection of free sessions plus a free trial of their paid prepares, with most of the library behind a subscription. Insight Timer works the other way around: the bulk of its catalog is free, with a paid MemberPlus tier for extras like courses and offline listening.

To choose the right meditation app, start with your main goal, whether that’s stress relief, better sleep, or a guided start as a beginner. From there, check prices and any features you care about, like offline listening or language options. Then take advantage of the free trials. Most apps offer one, and it’s a good way to see how an app fits before you pay. While you’re trying it out, sample a few different narrators. A lot of meditation comes down to the voice guiding you, and finding someone you connect with can turn the practice into something you look forward to.

It has been revealed that calm is worth it if you want to ease stress and anxiety, sleep better, focus when your mind wanders, or learn the basics of meditation. The app may be a helpful way to build a daily mental health habit, with support for moments from a racing mind at bedtime to a hard day at work. Whether you need quick relief in the moment or ongoing support through a life change, Calm is for you.

You can try a 7-day free trial to see how it fits your flow, and you don’t need to know which content format you prefer ahead of time.

Calm and Headspace have a lot in common. Both offer guided meditation, beginner-friendly courses, short sessions for when stress spikes, sleep content, and mindful movement. The difference is in the mix and the overall feel. On Calm, you’ll find hundreds of Sleep Stories read by well-known voices, daily meditations from a rotating cast of instructors, music, soundscapes, and Emergency Calm sessions for high-stress moments. On Headspace, you’ll find a more course-led, step-by-step approach and an AI companion called Ebb. Both offer free content and a free trial, so the best way to decide is to try each and see which feels right for you.

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

Growing Older on the Spectrum: The Unique Needs of Autistic Adults

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Because so few studies focus on aging in autistic adults, there is little understanding—and support—for the specialized needs they may have later in life.
  • According to recent reports, our understanding of autism has evolved considerably over the last 50 years.
  • But even as our understanding has grown, we still know very little about the unique needs and challenges of autistic people in midlife and beyond, or about the supports that help most.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Because so few studies focus on aging in autistic adults, there is little understanding—and support—for the specialized needs they may have later in life.

According to recent reports, our understanding of autism has evolved considerably over the last 50 years. Today, many autistic adults who were overlooked or misdiagnosed in childhood are finally pursuing a proper evaluation and diagnosis.

But even as our understanding has grown, we still know very little about the unique needs and challenges of autistic people in midlife and beyond, or about the supports that help most. Why? Because less than 1 percent of all indexed autism research has focused on midlife and older age.

That means we still don’t understand the cognitive, health, and social experiences of autistic adults as they age. And this lack of research influences clinical practice: Historically, clinicians haven’t been trained and equipped with an understanding of autism in older age.

An analysis of health records from the United Kingdom indicates that around 90 percent of autistic people in midlife (ages 40 to 59), and 96 percent of older adults (ages 60 and beyond), are undiagnosed.1 Until autism research and diagnosis rates improve, we won’t understand the full autistic experience, but here are the truths coming into focus.

[Read: “How Can I Get Evaluated for Autism as an Adult?”].

Autism in older age is associated with complex health needs. Compared with the general population, middle-aged and older autistic adults have higher rates of several physical and mental health conditions, making frequent and proactive screenings notable for this group.

Despite the higher rates of dementia, Parkinson’s disease, and cognitive difficulties found among autistic adults, we should not assume that autism is linked to accelerated cognitive aging. Autistic people are no more likely to experience rapid cognitive aging than are members of the general population, according to research.

In a recent development, however, one study found that about 20 percent of autistic people had highly variable cognitive profiles; this subgroup developed an old-age profile earlier than expected compared to non-autistic adults. For these individuals, red flags for cognitive decline and dementia may present at a younger age than we’d expect in the general population. Autistic adults who fit this profile may require additional help and support as they age to remain safe and independent.

Sleep typically deteriorates with age, however, adults with high autistic traits are more likely than others to report moderate or severe sleep problems as they grow older, including problems with falling and staying asleep, sleep efficiency, and daytime tiredness.

It has been revealed that sleep is a lynchpin for general and mental health. Sleep problems, for example, tend to worsen anxiety, a condition that is highly prevalent among autistic adults. Improving sleep quality by blocking out light with curtains, using earplugs or a white noise machine, choosing pajamas and bedsheets made from soothing fabrics, and/or using a weighted blanket can significantly benefit the mental health of autistic people as they age.

[Read: This is Why You’re Always Tired].

Industry observers note that sensory processing differences are part of the autistic experience. Over a lifetime, exposure to difficult and unpleasant sensory experiences, like crowded, noisy environments, is linked to mental health problems in older autistic adults. At the same time, even small changes, such as noise-canceling headphones or wearing a face mask in public, can help. Adjustments and accommodations such as these should not be overlooked when thinking of health and quality of life.

Compared with non-autistic people, autistic adults experience higher rates of loneliness — the subjective feeling of lacking meaningful connection. While middle-aged and older autistic people tend to have small social networks, about one in five autistic adults has no contact with family or friends in a given month, compared with one in 20 neurotypical adults. Certain neurodivergent traits — rigidity, flat affect or an aloof personality, and communication challenges — may help explain social difficulties.

Interestingly, in the general population, we found that women tend to be lonelier than men. In the autistic population, the feeling of loneliness was more common in men.

Recent findings suggest that connections with family and friends seem to provide a protective mental health benefit and lead to a better quality of life. Supporting autistic people in forming meaningful relationships on their own terms and in relation to their passions and interests could be a key target for interventions.

#137905. Breaking: What Bystanders Can Do to Stop Sexual Violence

Breaking: What Bystanders Can Do to Stop Sexual Violence

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as an undergrad student decades ago, I attended a dorm presentation describing the importance of giving and receiving sexual consent.
  • A high-profile athlete on campus raised his hand and said, in utter disbelief, “That can’t be right.
  • I was horrified by his comment, but most students laughed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as an undergrad student decades ago, I attended a dorm presentation describing the importance of giving and receiving sexual consent. The workshop leaders explained that if your partner noted “no” or “stop” but you proceeded to have sex anyway, it was considered rape.

A high-profile athlete on campus raised his hand and said, in utter disbelief, “That can’t be right. By that definition, everyone I’ve ever had sex with I’ve raped.”.

I was horrified by his comment, but most students laughed. He clearly saw nothing wrong with the view he’d expressed, presumably believing it was widely shared.

Industry observers note that I immediately thought of this experience when I heard about the alleged sexual assault committed by seven fraternity members at Cornell University. As a social psychologist, and the author of a book examining why so-called good people stay silent in the face of problematic behavior, what I find most tragic about the events at Cornell is that reportedly over 50 men on a group chat learned about the assault as it was happening. Yet there’s been no public report that any of them tried to stop the assault, help the victim, or contact campus or local police departments.

This type of inaction is very common. In about one-third of sexual assaults, at least one other person is present who potentially could intervene but in most instances chooses not to. Why?

Recent findings suggest that data suggests a minority of men actually commit sexual assault. Researchers estimate about 6.5% of male college students in the United States and Canada have committed rape. Yet many men who find sexual violence offensive mistakenly believe that other men do not.

Undergraduate men in one study reported their beliefs about common rape myths, such as “If a girl doesn’t physically fight back, you can’t really say it was rape,” and “If a girl goes to a room alone with a guy at a party, it is her own fault if she is raped.” Researchers then asked participants how they thought both their close friends and average male college students would answer these same questions.

The results provided clear evidence that college men have skewed views of what those around them are thinking. Most students saw their classmates and friends as more supportive of rape myths than they themselves were.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, believing that other men generally accept sexual violence—even when this belief is wrong—inhibits their willingness to intervene to stop such behavior when they encounter it. In fact, men’s beliefs about their peers’ attitudes are a stronger predictor of their willingness to intervene than their own stated attitudes about sexual aggression.

Sources indicate that men who underestimate their peers’ discomfort with sexually aggressive behavior often fear the consequences of calling out problematic views or intervening in the face of inappropriate behavior. The most common reason male college students give for failing to intervene in situations involving sexual violence is a fear of being laughed at or ridiculed—in particular, a desire not to appear weak to other men.

It has been revealed that men who actually commit assault also tend to overestimate support for such behavior. Not surprisingly, men who report having committed sexual assault believe that other men are more accepting of such behavior and have engaged in such behavior themselves.

This assumed support leads them to feel comfortable describing problematic behavior, which leads other men to believe that sexual violence is more common, and more accepted, than it actually is.

Industry observers note that given the consistent evidence that men wrongly believe that most men are more comfortable with sexual violence than they themselves are, the challenge is not to change the social norm. It’s getting people to see what it actually already is.

Correcting such misperceptions can go a long way toward reducing sexual violence. First-year male college students who participate in a 90-minute sexual assault prevention program—focused on refuting rape myths, increasing awareness of the importance of consent, and correcting misperceptions about other men’s attitudes and behaviors—report reduced levels of sexual aggression themselves four months later.

Industry observers note that these programs work in two ways. First, men who receive accurate information about what other men actually believe are less inhibited about speaking out and intervening. Second, men who are at risk of engaging in sexual aggression may change their intentions after learning that their peers do not support such behavior.

At the same time, men in tight-knit groups feel considerable pressure to show loyalty to other group members, which may lead to ignoring bad behavior committed by their peers.

It has been revealed that but the underlying dynamics of peer influence can help shift group norms from protecting group members by staying silent to stepping in to prevent bad behavior. One college football player described looking out for his teammates, even if that meant interrupting a potential sexual encounter: “Maybe you don’t get the girl, but you’ll keep your scholarship and still be on the team.”.

It has been revealed that another approach for preventing sexual assault is to learn strategies for intervening. Bystander intervention programs emphasize the importance of stopping bad behavior before it escalates, teach specific skills for intervening, and remind people that everyone has a responsibility to prevent sexual violence.

Sources indicate that students who participate in such programs are more confident in their ability to intervene and more willing to do so. Most importantly, rates of sexual violence are markedly lower on campuses that have implemented these programs. For example, one study found that experiences of sexual harassment and stalking were 11% lower and that instances of unwanted sexual activity with women who were too drunk or high to stop them were as much as 17% lower.

Industry observers note that it’s tempting to read about the Cornell case and assume the apparent inaction in the face of problematic behavior is uniquely a problem at one college, or only with members of fraternities, or only with college students. But the reality is that pretty much everyone has been in situations where they’ve seen potentially problematic behavior and failed to speak up.

Understanding the very normal psychological factors that lead people to misperceive what others are actually thinking and feeling—and learning specific strategies for intervening—can make a real difference.

Pen in hand, card open, and all you've got is “Happy birthday.” Birthday wishes should come naturally, right? But putting your feelings into words can be hard.

Nobody wants a message that comes off as too stiff or too cheesy, either. And, of course, birthday greetings for different people—whether it's your best friend, your little sister, or a work colleague—should sound different, since your relationships with them are, too.

Industry observers note that don’t worry, we’re here to help you say exactly what you mean without going overboard. Keep reading to find 100 birthday wishes and greetings for your friends, family, and coworkers, including short happy birthday wishes you can text or drop into a card. You’ll also get tips to make them your own.

Friends are the family you choose… or the people who accidentally become family after you’ve spent a year learning all of their deepest, darkest secrets. These are the people you know you have to create the ultimate birthday wish for. After all, they know all your most embarrassing moments and still choose to be there for you through it all.

Whether you’re celebrating someone you’ve known since high school or a newer connection that just gets you, here are 30 birthday wishes that range from soft and sentimental to chaotic and hilarious.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Everything you love about enchiladas, minus the fuss!
  • This easy, nourishing dish features tender cubed sweet potato or winter squash, fiber- & protein-rich black beans, and a rich red enchilada sauce.
  • In a recent development, it’s believed that enchiladas may have originated from a similar Mayan dish called papadzules.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Everything you love about enchiladas, minus the fuss! This super flavorful, cheesy vegan enchilada skillet comes together in about 30 minutes with simple methods, minimal dishes, and no need to fill or roll tortillas.

This easy, nourishing dish features tender cubed sweet potato or winter squash, fiber- & protein-rich black beans, and a rich red enchilada sauce. Everything gets simmered in 1 pan and topped with a melty cashew “cheese” that makes it SUPER satisfying and delicious!

In a recent development, it’s believed that enchiladas may have originated from a similar Mayan dish called papadzules. But the first written recipe for enchiladas was in an 1831 cookbook called El Cocinero mexicano. Typically, enchiladas are made with meat, seafood, beans, cheese, potatoes, or vegetables stuffed in corn tortillas and topped with enchilada sauce.

Our “inspired-by” enchilada skillet has all the flavors of classic enchiladas, but it’s vegan, and instead of rolling the filling in tortillas, we slice the tortillas and cook everything together in one pan on the stovetop!

Industry observers note that this 1-pan, 30-minute vegan enchilada skillet begins with a base of sautéed vegetables — onion, garlic, sweet potato, and poblano pepper. The veggies are flexible here, so feel free to experiment! We love kabocha squash for a fall variation and have found green bell peppers work well when poblanos aren’t available. We also think butternut squash would be nice, as would greens such as kale or spinach.

Once the onions are very tender and the squash and peppers are just beginning to soften, we stir in black beans + corn tortillas that have been sliced into strips.

Next comes the final ingredient in the skillet portion of this dish (hello, simple + flavorful!): red enchilada sauce. We love the bold flavor of our homemade enchilada sauce (and usually have it stocked in the freezer), but this recipe also works well with store-bought enchilada sauce.

Sources indicate that and lastly, it just wouldn’t be enchiladas without: the CHEESE! More specifically, a flavorful cashew “cheese” sauce inspired by our fan favorite Cheesy Vegan Pizza Beans. It’s made by blending up cashews, water, lime juice, garlic, tapioca starch, and sea salt. When poured over the enchilada skillet and covered with a lid, the heat and tapioca starch do their magic, creating a melty, cheesy layer! Total swoon!

It has been revealed that we highly recommend trying the cashew “cheese” sauce, even if you’re not vegan or dairy-free! It’s super easy and takes this dish to a whole newly introduced level. However, this enchilada skillet is also delicious with shredded vegan or dairy cheese (such as pepper jack).

Recent findings suggest that we think you’ll LOVE this recipe! It’s:SmokySpicySuper flavorfulSatisfyingVersatileQuick & easy to make& SO delicious!

This dish is hearty and amazing as a standalone quick meal for weeknights! It would also pair well with our Smoky Shredded Tofu Taco “Meat” or 1-Pan Mexican Shredded Chicken for a higher-protein option. Or, for more veggies, try it with our Crunchy Jicama Slaw or Quick Citrusy Cabbage Slaw.

According to recent reports, if you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Neurodivergent kids aren’t the only ones who struggle with changing routines or new life phases. Adults can feel overwhelmed by transitions, too.

Whether starting a latest job, moving to a new town, or sending a child off to college, transitions are equal parts exciting and uncomfortable for neurodivergent individuals.

The struggle often looks different in children and adults, but the demand is much the same: Stop what you are doing, shift your attention, figure out the next step, manage your emotions, and move into a different role, task, place, or expectation. The bigger the transition, the harder it feels.

Typical transitions include returning to work after a vacation, adjusting to a new schedule, shifting from work to parenting mode, navigating relationship changes, and recovering from illness or injury.

[Free Download: Get Control of Your Life and Schedule].

Recent findings suggest that from the outside, the response of an adult with ADHD may look like procrastination, avoidance, irritability, disorganization, or poor follow-through. Internally, they are likely dealing with anxiety, emotional overload, decision fatigue, time blindness, or the frustration of knowing exactly what needs to be done but struggling to begin.

“I struggle so badly with transitions (they feel almost literally painful) that I spend up to five hours in a state of crippling inertia before handling a task that needs to be done,” wrote one woman with ADHD in a social media post, pleading for help.

Transitions can be especially difficult when they involve uncertainty. A new job may bring excitement and anxiety about performance. A vacation may feel adventurous and overwhelming. Even a positive life change can feel unsettling when structure falls away.

It has been revealed that “I don’t travel much,” says Layla, an ADDitude reader from California. “Transitions are hard for me.”.

[Get This Free Download: Finish Your To-Do List Today].

Shave the rough edges off transitions by doing the following seven things:.

Most importantly, adults with ADHD should keep in mind that embracing change easily is not necessarily a sign of maturity. Feelings of anxiety around transitions may just mean that your brain needs more preview, structure, recovery, and support to move from one demand to the next.

For How Long Do You Need to Meditate?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, picture this: 71 adults signed up for a study comparing brief to longer mindfulness practice.
  • Participants were divided at random into three groups: One group got 20 minutes of mindfulness meditation, a second group got five minutes, and the control group relaxed with audiobook excerpts from Bill Bryson’s A Short History of Nearly Everything, Bryson’s soothing recounting of the cosmos and our place in it.
  • In studies like these, “mindfulness meditation” typically means sitting quietly, eyes closed or softened, resting nonjudgmental attention on your breath or bodily sensations, gently noticing when your mind wanders (as it will), and just as gently bringing it back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, picture this: 71 adults signed up for a study comparing brief to longer mindfulness practice. Many had never meditated, while others had dabbled years before.

Participants were divided at random into three groups: One group got 20 minutes of mindfulness meditation, a second group got five minutes, and the control group relaxed with audiobook excerpts from Bill Bryson’s A Short History of Nearly Everything, Bryson’s soothing recounting of the cosmos and our place in it.

In studies like these, “mindfulness meditation” typically means sitting quietly, eyes closed or softened, resting nonjudgmental attention on your breath or bodily sensations, gently noticing when your mind wanders (as it will), and just as gently bringing it back.

Industry observers note that now, you might expect that longer meditations would deliver greater benefits. After all, we’re conditioned to believe that more is better—especially when it comes to self-improvement. But this research and many other studies find that more minutes don’t necessarily mean more benefit: Shorter practices can work just as well—and sometimes better—while consistency may matter more than duration.

Industry observers note that in this first study, each participant attended four 25-minute sessions over two weeks. In every session, the time not spent on audio-guided mindfulness-of-breath practice was filled by Bryson’s eloquence. To ensure the results reflected only the study activities, participants were asked to avoid any formal mindfulness practices outside these sessions.

According to recent reports, after those two weeks, the five-minute meditators actually highlighted greater improvements in stress and mindful awareness (the tendency to stay present in daily life with less judgement) than the 20-minute group. Even depression and anxiety improved just as much—if not more.

Was the extra time with Bryson the magic ingredient for those five-minute meditators? The control group, who luxuriated in 25 uninterrupted minutes of his charm, indicated no meaningful improvement. So while his voice may soothe, it wasn’t what moved the needle.

One five-minute meditator put it this way: “I always thought that to do mindfulness, I’d need a long time to dedicate to this, which seemed too challenging to even start. But I’ve learned that five minutes can help!” In contrast, a 20-minute participant admitted, “I think a shorter one would be better for me to learn mindfulness.”.

In a recent development, there’s more. The facilitator observed that participants in the 20-minute meditation sessions more often fidgeted, shifted in their seats, and peeked through half-closed eyes, as if tranquility were just out of reach. Meanwhile, the five-minute meditators appeared more at ease and less prone to these signs of discomfort. Five of them even requested recordings to continue at home. The 20-minute group? Not a single request. For these beginners, less really did seem to be more.

Sources indicate that now, before you dash off to cancel that meditation retreat, remember that this study focused on people with little to no meditation experience. So if you’re a seasoned meditator, those longer sessions might still pack more punch for you, as we’ll explore later. And both the five-minute and 20-minute groups demonstrated improvements in mindful awareness, depression, anxiety, and stress compared to the control group. The five-minute meditators just improved more when it came to mindful awareness and stress.

The takeaway? For beginners, a quick dip into mindfulness might be more refreshing than a long soak.

You might be wondering, Isn’t this just one study? Could it be a fluke? But multiple randomized controlled trials have explored how the length of meditation shapes its impact.

I join Christine Carter, Ph.D, in a webinar next week to talk about my book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick.

In a recent development, in the largest of these studies, researchers recruited 372 adults online—about half of them latest to meditation—to see how the “dose” of mindfulness meditation affected mindful awareness and emotional well-being. Participants were randomly sorted into one of four groups: Some meditated for 10 minutes, others for 20, and the rest listened to a 10- or 20-minute National Geographic article on sequoia trees. (Because nothing soothes stress like a deep dive into bark thickness.).

According to recent reports, what did the researchers find? The 10-minute meditators highlighted greater improvements in mindful awareness than those who listened to the 10-minute sequoia lecture. Surprisingly, the 20-minute meditation group didn’t outperform any group—not even the tree enthusiasts. In fact, the 10-minute group showed slightly greater improvements in mindful awareness than the 20-minute meditators, although the difference wasn’t statistically significant, meaning it could have occurred by chance. Still, it suggests that for boosting mindful awareness right after practice, 10 minutes might be at least as effective as 20.

It has been revealed that but that was just one session. What happens with consistent practice? In another study, 77 college students were randomly assigned to meditate daily for 10 or 20 minutes. After two weeks, both groups highlighted similar improvements in stress and, again, mindful awareness. But those assigned to the 20-minute group experienced a slightly greater boost in self-compassion, the skill of meeting your own struggles with the kindness you’d offer a dear friend.

Industry observers note that so if you’ve poured hours into longer meditations, you can rest easy—it wasn’t for nothing. The evidence suggests that whether your sessions are short or sustained, they can offer meaningful benefits.

Another notable finding is that the 10-minute group practiced more consistently, logging about 82 minutes total. The 20-minute group missed more days and didn’t always finish, ending up with just 103. Double the goal, barely a quarter more practice.

If you’ve ever tried meditating, you might be nodding along. Some sessions are bliss, while others are a tug-of-war with time. Maybe you’ve battled that nagging frustration, trying to keep your mind steady for more than a fleeting moment. Or felt the magnetic pull of distraction, your mind wandering just when you need it to stay put. As the minutes crawl, doubt can creep in: Am I even doing this right? Is it worth it? These tough moments can teach you a lot, but they can also make meditation feel intimidating—and make you less likely to stick with it, especially when you’re just starting out. Another study looked at even longer sessions, comparing 10 minutes of meditation to 30 minutes. This experiment split 161 adults into four groups: 10 or 30 minutes of daily sitting meditation, or the same amount of mindful movement. The mindful movement was a stretching practice that brings mindful awareness into motion—less stillness, same presence.

Recent findings suggest that after two weeks, everyone saw benefits: Mindful awareness increased, well-being improved, and distress levels dropped. But there were no significant differences among the groups. Whether they meditated for 10 minutes or 30, sitting or moving, all the groups seemed to benefit equally.

So, here’s the bottom line: One study found that longer sessions more strongly boosted self-compassion. Another showed that shorter ones more effectively reduced stress. But across studies, most of the key benefits—mindful awareness, mental health, well-being—weren’t tied to how long people practiced.

Why? Because as we’ll keep exploring, the nervous system learns through repetition, not duration. It’s consistency that reshapes patterns. Not heroic efforts once in a while, but showing up, again and again, however you can.

Recent findings suggest that the benefits of consistency over length show up in observational studies, too, where people choose how often and how long to meditate. While observational studies can’t pin down cause and effect, they offer a richer view of how shorter practices play out in the real world.

In a recent development, imagine it’s early morning. You reach for your phone and open Insight Timer, a free meditation app. Before your meditation, it asks, “How are you today?” You tap an icon—maybe “OK,” maybe “great”—capturing a snapshot of your mood in seconds.

Now imagine doing this regularly, for 14 months straight. That’s exactly what 10,409 people from 103 countries did in a groundbreaking study. Many were new to meditation, using the app to track their emotional ups and downs in real time. It’s like taking your emotional temperature—not with a thermometer, but with a single tap that sums up how you feel.

The findings? Consistency (four to seven days a week)—not duration—was the strongest predictor of better mood, resilience, and equanimity, the ability to stay cool under pressure. Think of it like watering a plant: A little each week keeps it happy and growing. Forget all month and drown it after four weeks? It wilts anyway.

Recent findings suggest that for beginners in the Insight Timer study, short sessions—five to 10 minutes—outshone longer ones in improving mood over time. But after 20 sessions? Longer practices—21 to 30 minutes—began to take the lead in mood improvement. It’s like your brain needs to build its meditation muscles before longer sessions feel better than short ones—like a marathon that only gives you the high once you’ve earned it.

Sources indicate that but do shorter sessions lose their impact as you gain experience? Not at all. They might just become your secret weapon. After 80 sessions, shorter practices make a late-game comeback, boosting equanimity and showing that even seasoned meditators can benefit from briefer sessions.

The idea that consistency beats duration is backed by a meta-analysis challenging the belief that longer equals better. Think of a meta-analysis as a “study of studies,” combining data from multiple research papers to uncover clearer, substantial-picture insights.

When researchers analyzed 203 randomized controlled trials totaling 15,971 participants, they found no association between meditation session length and better outcomes. In fact, a trend emerged in favor of shorter practices for reducing depression symptoms, although it wasn’t statistically significant. Still, shorter sessions were at least as effective as longer ones, calling into question the assumption that more minutes always mean more benefits. So what’s the takeaway? When you’re starting out, don’t sweat the long stuff. Quick sessions might do more to lift your mood early on. As you settle in, longer practices might bring deeper emotional gains. But even if you’re a pro, short sessions don’t lose their value—they just shift their superpower, helping you stay steady when life throws you curveballs. Different strengths, different stages. And who doesn’t love a shortcut that actually works?

Eli Susman, Ph.D., is a UC Berkeley-trained psychologist, former Harvard researcher, and author of Micropractice: A Science-Backed Approach for Calm, Clarity, and Joy in 30 Seconds or Less, forthcoming in 22 languages.

  • It has been revealed that it’s Christmas morning.
  • Sources indicate that maybe you’re single, estranged or far from family, working the holiday, grieving, or just not in the mood to celebrate.
  • In a recent development, in fact, there are plenty of ways to make the day your own.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

It has been revealed that it’s Christmas morning. The street outside is still, your phone hasn’t buzzed with plans, and the whole day is wide open, with no schedule and no one to check in with. It might feel like a relief, or it might ache. Sometimes it’s both in the same hour.

Sources indicate that maybe you’re single, estranged or far from family, working the holiday, grieving, or just not in the mood to celebrate. But no matter why you’re spending Christmas alone, the day can still feel warm and full.

In a recent development, in fact, there are plenty of ways to make the day your own. Here you’ll find ideas for staying in or going out, plus what to do if it gets hard.

If you’re spending Christmas on your own, you’re far from the only one. More people live alone than ever, and plenty of people simply prefer a quiet holiday.

Recent findings suggest that with that in mind, being alone and feeling lonely aren't the same thing. Being alone is a circumstance: no one else is around. Loneliness is a feeling of disconnection, and it can show up at a packed holiday table or an empty house.

In a recent development, so what makes time alone feel good rather than lonely? A massive factor may be whether you have a say in how you spend it. In three studies where people reported on their moments throughout the day, time alone felt more positive when people chose it for themselves.

If you didn’t choose to be alone this Christmas, it’s okay if that stings. What you do with the day is still up to you.

Whether you’re in the mood for a slow day under a blanket, time out among people, or a bit of both, you don’t owe anyone an explanation for how you spend your day.

If you’d rather stay in, here are a few ways to make the day at home feel comforting.

It has been revealed that 1. Start the morning with meditation or journaling: Settle into a comfortable position and let your eyes close or soften. Tune into your breath and the sensations in your body. When thoughts about the day ahead drift in, notice them, then gently return to your breath. Journaling is another way to check in with how you’re feeling.

In a recent development, 💙 Want some guidance for those few minutes? Settle into the Mornings meditation on Calm.

2. Cook or order the meal you really want: Skip the turkey-and-trimmings unless you love them. Go for whatever you're craving, whether that’s a roast for one, pancakes at noon, or your go-to takeout. Choosing food you’re excited about can turn an ordinary meal into a treat.

💙 Listen to Piano for Rainy Days: Nice & Cozy while you cook.

It has been revealed that 4. Do a movie marathon on your own terms: You get to choose what you watch, and no one talks through the good parts. Line up your favorite holiday films, or skip the Christmas theme entirely and binge the series you’ve been saving.

Recent findings suggest that 5. Get lost in a book or an audiobook: A long, quiet day is a great chance to sink into a story without interruption. If your eyes get tired, switch to an audiobook while you putter around or lie on the couch.

💙 Discover ten self-love activities to improve your well-being.

If you’d like to spend the day out of the house, these ideas include solo outings and activities around other people. Holiday hours often change and volunteer spots fill up, so check details as early as you can..

6. Spend time somewhere green: Stroll along a park path or trail, or find a bench and settle in for a while. Time in green space has been shown to quiet a busy mind. In one study, adults who walked for 90 minutes in nature reported less rumination (the looping, negative thinking that can feed low moods) than those who walked along a busy road.

Industry observers note that 💙 Ready to step outside? Try Calm’s Nature Walk meditation with Dr. Eric López to soak in the sights, sounds, and smells around you.

7. Volunteer for a few hours: Soup kitchens, shelters, and animal rescues often need extra hands on Christmas Day. Volunteering connects you with people who share a purpose, and research suggests performing acts of kindness may boost your well-being.

💙 Feeling the urge to give back? Tune into the Random Acts of Kindness meditation on Calm to see how small gestures add up.

Recent findings suggest that 8. Join a community meal or gathering: Many community centers and local groups host open Christmas meals. It’s a low-pressure way to share the day with others, even if only for a couple of hours.

Recent findings suggest that 9. Find somewhere that’s open: Movie theaters, some cafés and restaurants, and hotel lounges often keep holiday hours. Even a little time around other people, strangers included, can bring a touch of connection to your day.

10. Take a day trip: Head to a nearby town, hike a upcoming trail, or visit a spot you’ve been meaning to see. A change of scenery can make the day feel like an occasion.

There are many ways to make a quiet day feel less lonely, from a quick text to a mindfulness practice. Choose whichever of these appeal to you.

Industry observers note that send a text, leave a voice note, or call someone you care about. If loved ones are far away, you could:.

Schedule a call in advance, especially if you’re in different time zones.

Do an activity together over video, like cooking or watching a movie.

Ask for a family recipe, make it, and share how it turned out.

Sources indicate that you can start a tradition on your own. Keep it small and simple, such as a letter to your future self you open next year or a movie you rewatch every December 25.

💙 Not sure where to start? Explore Redefining Traditions with therapist Kati Morton on Calm.

According to recent reports, if you feel loneliness creeping in, a loving-kindness meditation may help you feel more connected. In one study, people who did a short loving-kindness meditation reported more feelings of social connection toward strangers than those who did a control task.

💙 Press play on the Loving-Kindness meditation on Calm.

In a recent development, give yourself one thing to look forward to after your shift, such as a comfort meal or a call with someone you love. Treat yourself during the day with a good coffee or a walk on your break. You can also celebrate with others on another day, and it’s just as meaningful.

💙 If you’re still feeling lonely after the holiday, here are seven tips to deal with loneliness.

Recent findings suggest that even if you’ve chosen to be alone, Christmas can bring up emotions like sadness, envy, or grief. Here’s how to work through them.

Other people’s picture-perfect holiday photos can leave you feeling like you’re missing out. Try stepping away from your phone for a few hours. Those posts are a highlight reel, and the rest of their day rarely looks as polished.

If the feeling lingers, try self-compassion: meeting yourself with the same warmth you’d offer a friend who’s feeling down. In a review of studies, people who practiced self-compassion reported lower anxiety, depression, and stress than people who didn’t. You could tell yourself, “This is hard, but I’m doing my best, and that’s enough.”.

💙 Practice being a Friend on the Inside with Jeff Warren on Calm.

In a recent development, if you’re missing someone this Christmas, the day can feel especially tender. You can honor them in subtle ways: cook their favorite dish, light a candle in their memory, or write them a letter. There’s no right way to grieve, so let the day be as quiet or as full as you need.

It’s okay to keep some distance from family on Christmas if you need to. Calls and replies are optional, and so is explaining your choice. You can mute the group chat for the day if that brings you some peace.

If someone asks what you’re up to, you could say, “I’m keeping it low-key this year.” Whatever comes up, mixed feelings included, you don’t have to push it aside just because it’s the holidays.

According to recent reports, if your sadness lingers past the holiday, disrupts your sleep or appetite, or leaves you feeling hopeless, talk to a doctor or someone you trust. If you’re in the U.S. and need support right away, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. If you’re outside the U.S., findahelpline.com lists free local services.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re alone for Christmas, it can help to give the day some structure. Pick one or two things that excite you, such as a comfort meal, a long walk, or a movie, and let the rest of the day unfold naturally. A quick call or text with a loved one can be a nice touch, too.

According to recent reports, it’s normal to want to spend Christmas alone. After a long or busy year, a quiet day can be restful, and preferring it doesn’t mean anything is wrong. Plan the day around what appeals to you.

If you’d rather not stay home on Christmas, there are plenty of places to spend the day. Look for open movie theaters, cafés, and parks nearby, or join a community meal at a local center. You could also volunteer for an organization to meet people while contributing to a cause. Holiday hours vary, so it’s worth confirming before you head out.

According to recent reports, if you’re single on Christmas, the day is yours to spend however you want. You could cook something you love, explore a upcoming spot, or go for a casual meal or movie with friends.

Industry observers note that if you’re feeling sad or lonely on Christmas, let yourself feel those emotions without judgment. Consider reaching out to a loved one, even briefly. A short meditation can also bring some relief. If the sadness feels overwhelming or won’t lift, speak to a doctor or someone you trust.

It’s okay to skip Christmas altogether. You can treat December 25 as an ordinary day: rest, work, or do something unrelated to the holiday. If the season stirs up grief or stress, stepping back from holiday looks is one way to look after yourself.

A solo tradition can be anything that brings you comfort, whether that’s a special breakfast, a journal entry, or a new ornament you pick out every year. A simple tradition is more likely to stick from year to year.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“What helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s.”.

The experience of ADHD in midlife and older age is largely undocumented but not unimportant.

An estimated 66% of adults with ADHD ages 45 to 54 have no recorded diagnosis, according to an analysis of UK health records. Missed diagnoses and misdiagnoses make research on this population difficult — but not impossible.

Amber John, Ph.D., a researcher at the University of Liverpool, reviewed studies on how the experience of ADHD changes with age during her November 2026 ADDitude webinar, “Aging with ADHD: Newly introduced Research Findings in Midlife and Beyond.”.

Below are some of the themes John highlighted and what they suggest about the support adults with ADHD need in midlife and beyond.

In clinical interviews, adults with ADHD recalled feeling different growing up but being unable to explain why. A diagnosis helped them see those experiences in a different light.

It has been revealed that “These experiences that previously might have seemed disconnected, for many, started to form this more understandable pattern,” John said. “And that could really change the meaning that someone gives to those past experiences, particularly where they had just been viewed as evidence of personal failings.”.

[Read: The Transformative Power of an ADHD Diagnosis for Older Women].

According to recent reports, many people with ADHD develop painstaking routines and coping strategies to manage symptoms. The effort it takes to keep those routines going often goes unseen and can fuel burnout.

Industry observers note that “This raises a really key question about what it is that we actually mean when we say someone is functioning well,” John said. “Understanding someone’s support needs really means that we need to ask about the cost of managing.”.

Industry observers note that the experience of ADHD changes as life circumstances change. Menopause, caring for aging parents, and retirement can affect how symptoms play out in daily life and disrupt routines that have helped people cope for decades.

“A way that somebody is using to manage or to cope that’s worked in one period of life might become less useful when health, or demands, or available support changes,” John stated.

Sources indicate that [Read: I Feared I Had Alzheimer’s. It Turns Out It Was Undiagnosed ADHD.].

Sources indicate that in doctors’ offices and workplaces, people with ADHD often shoulder the burden of explaining their needs and advocating for basic support. They can put considerable effort into managing their symptoms and still face barriers to getting care or participating at work.

“There is a limit to focusing on individual-level coping because a person can put really substantial effort into managing whilst the environment actually continues to make participation difficult,” John noted.

According to recent reports, john’s research highlights the need for ADHD support that adapts as people’s circumstances change. We shouldn’t assume that “what helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s,” she remarked.

Panic attack hangover: 12 ways to recover and feel better

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • Sources indicate that you’re finally on the other side of the panic attack.
  • The hours (or even days) after a panic episode can feel foggy and disorienting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Sources indicate that you’re finally on the other side of the panic attack. The chest tightness has eased, the shaking has stopped, and your breathing feels more steady. But instead of relief, there’s a strange exhaustion settling in, like you just ran a marathon you don’t remember signing up for. This is often called a panic attack hangover.

The hours (or even days) after a panic episode can feel foggy and disorienting. You might experience headaches, sore muscles, difficulty concentrating, or an overwhelming need to crash. These symptoms can feel alarming if no one ever mentioned they might show up, but they’re actually a normal part of the body’s recovery process.

Recent findings suggest that understanding what’s happening can ease some of the worry, and having a few gentle tools on hand can make the aftermath feel a little less isolating. Here’s what to know about panic attack hangovers, along with research-backed tips to support yourself through them.

Recent findings suggest that A panic attack hangover is the period of lingering after-effects that follow a panic attack. Even though the rush of fear and physical symptoms has eased, your body can still feel off-balance for hours or even days afterward. Many people describe it as feeling strangely similar to an alcohol hangover: foggy, heavy, and emotionally sensitive.

According to recent reports, the experience can be unsettling, especially if you didn’t expect panic to have an “aftermath.” But panic attack hangovers are both common and temporary. They’re simply your body’s way of recovering from an intense stress response.

Note: This guide focuses on panic attacks. If you’ve had an anxiety attack, which builds more gradually, read How to manage symptoms and find ease after an anxiety attack instead.

Sources indicate that while panic attack hangovers can happen at any time, the effects aren’t the same for everyone. Still, there are some common symptoms people notice after a panic attack, some more frequently than others.

Fatigue or exhaustion: You might feel like your body’s battery has been completely drained.

Brain fog: You could find it hard to focus, remember things, or think clearly.

Muscle tension or soreness: Your jaw, shoulders, or chest might feel tight, achy, or tender from holding too much stress.

Emotional sensitivity: You may notice yourself crying more easily or feeling unusually fragile in everyday situations.

Headaches: You might experience pressure or pain often triggered by stress, shallow breathing, or unconscious clenching.

Digestive issues: You could have nausea, stomach discomfort, or sudden changes in your appetite that don’t seem to track.

Sleepiness or difficulty sleeping: You may find yourself crashing hard into deep rest or lying awake because you’re unable to settle down.

Industry observers note that these symptoms usually fade within a day, although they can last longer depending on the amount of sleep you get, your stress levels, and your overall health. If they’re frequent or overwhelming, though, it may be a sign to get additional support.

The reason panic leaves a hangover comes down to how your body handles stress. A panic attack sends your nervous system into full alert: your heart races, your breath quickens, and your muscles tighten. This is an ancient survival mechanism that’s been designed to keep you safe in an emergency.

In a recent development, the problem? Even when the threat isn’t real, your body still goes through the motions without an outlet to use up that surge of energy.

Once the attack ends, your system shifts into recovery mode. That crash can leave you feeling shaky, sore, and depleted… much like finishing an intense workout. On top of that, the emotional weight of the experience—fear, vulnerability, or the worry it might happen again—can keep your brain buzzing even while your body’s trying to rest.

This combination of physical exhaustion and emotional strain creates the foggy, heavy state that many people call a panic attack hangover.

According to recent reports, related read: Panic attack vs. anxiety attack? Here's the difference.

Industry observers note that panic attack hangovers can hit you hard, and you may not have the energy to do much after. These ideas are simple, low-lift, and designed for the days when everything feels like just too much.

Pick what’s doable today and ignore the rest: your nervous system will get the memo.

Your body just ran an internal marathon, and it’s important to be kind to it. If you can, postpone non-urgent tasks and try to give yourself a small recovery window.

Recent findings suggest that set a 10–15 minute timer, lie down or sit with support behind your back, and let your eyes rest. If you’re at work, try a short break, plus two minutes of slow breathing in a quiet corner. A pause can often help you recover faster.

Recent findings suggest that related read: Stressed and short on time? Here's how to try micro-meditation.

Industry observers note that staying hydrated and keeping your blood sugar steady can help you feel more balanced as your body recovers from a panic attack. Dehydration and dips in blood sugar can make fatigue, headaches, and brain fog worse.

Drink water or an electrolyte beverage and have a simple snack, like fruit with nut butter, yogurt, or toast. This helps give your system some fuel to reset.

Slow, gentle breathing tells your nervous system that you’re safe. Try this for 2–3 minutes: Inhale through your nose for four counts, and then exhale through pursed lips for six or eight.

Industry observers note that longer exhales can help your nervous system shift from fight-or-flight into rest-and-digest mode. But only do this if you feel comfortable. Don’t try to force anything.

💙 If you need some guidance, check out Reset with the Breath with Jay Shetty on the Calm app.

Panic can cause you to tighten your muscles, especially in the jaw, chest, shoulders, and hands. Short, light movements help clear it all without overexertion.

According to recent reports, you don’t have to do anything too intense. Simple shoulder rolls, gentle neck circles, a slow doorframe chest stretch, or a five-minute walk around the block or office floor can all help. If you’re seated, simply unclench your jaw, open and close your hands 10 times, or shake out your arms. The point is to loosen everything up.

According to recent reports, 💙 Need a little extra support? Try the Softening Anxiety Daily Move session with Mel Mah on the Calm app.

Quick temperature shifts, like splashing cool water on your face or holding something cold, can help ground you and interrupt the leftover jitters after a panic attack.

This is because it’s actually a form of grounding that allows your nervous system to anchor itself back to the present moment.

Related read: 18 grounding techniques to help relieve anxiety.

Decision fatigue amplifies the brain fog that comes after a panic attack, so try to cut down on the number of choices you’re making.

Trim your to-do list to one or two essentials, and choose “good enough” over perfect. Reheat leftovers instead of cooking, tell your coworkers you’re running a little behind, and move all noncritical tasks to the next day. It sounds simple, but having that space will help more than you know.

According to recent reports, reduce stimulation to ease the post-panic attack stress. Dim overhead lights, switch to warm lamps, lower the volume on any music or background noise, and silence non-urgent notifications on your phone and laptop for an hour.

Recent findings suggest that if noise is unavoidable, try earplugs or a brown-noise playlist. If you enjoy aromatherapy a familiar scent (like lavender, vanilla, or eucalyptus) can also be grounding.

Writing a few lines about your feelings and symptoms post-panic attack can help your brain process what happened and move forward. Research indicates that journaling supports emotional regulation, which is why so many people find it useful for panic recovery, too — even if it’s just a quick note or voice memo.

Recent findings suggest that consider reflecting on what triggered your attack, what symptoms you noticed, what helped calm you down, and what you could do differently next time. This can help give you more effective coping tools for future attacks.

Reaching out, even with a simple text, helps calm the nervous system. Social support is one of the strongest buffers for stress recovery.

In a recent development, send a text to someone you trust, simply asking to check in. If talking feels like too much, having someone just sit with you can also be helpful.

Related read: How to help someone having a panic attack (and what to avoid).

It has been revealed that after a panic attack, your system is more sensitive. Consider skipping or reducing how much caffeine you drink, as it can re-spark jitters. And avoid alcohol, as it’s been known to disrupt sleep and mood. Swap in decaf, herbal tea, or a half-caf and make sure to focus on nutrition and hydration to help support recovery.

Recent findings suggest that fatigue after a panic attack is real, and quality sleep helps reset your stress response. Keep bedtime predictable with a wind-down routine you enjoy, darken the room, and cool it slightly.

Recent findings suggest that if you desperately need a nap, cap it at 20–30 minutes, and avoid late-evening naps in order to protect nighttime sleep. If your mind spins when it’s time to go to bed, try a quiet meditation or body scan. This can help quiet the mind long enough to help you drift off faster.

💙 Fall asleep with ease thanks to the White Noise soundscape on the Calm app.

According to recent reports, even just knowing what you’ll do next time can take the edge off that heavy, shaky feeling that lingers after a panic attack. One simple idea? Make a three-step proposal that you keep on your phone or in your wallet.

Spend two minutes on long exhales or humming.

Splash cold water on your face or run cool water over your wrists.

It also helps to add one contact you trust to call or text.

While you may not be able to prevent every spiral, it always helps to have something in your back pocket (literally) that helps you feel less alone and more ready.

Yes, a hangover can sometimes trigger panic attacks. This is because alcohol disrupts sleep, dehydrates your body, and causes blood sugar swings — and all of these effects can make your nervous system more sensitive the next day.

Sources indicate that alcohol also interferes with the neurotransmitters that regulate your mood, which can amplify feelings of unease or dread. If you’re already prone to anxiety, that extra stress can tip into panic.

Every person who drinks won’t necessarily have a panic attack, but if you notice a pattern between hangovers and panic, it may help to cut back, hydrate more intentionally, or avoid drinking on nights before demanding days.

For most people, the hungover feeling eases within a few hours, but it’s not unusual for fatigue or brain fog to stretch into the next day. The duration of a panic attack hangover depends on several factors: how intense the panic attack was, how long it lasted, how well you slept, and what kind of support you gave your body afterward.

Try to find the recovery initiative that works best for you: getting enough water, food, gentle movement, and rest can speed up the reset. However, if you find that your hangover lasts longer than 24 hours or happens every time you panic, it may be a sign that your nervous system is under strain. In this case, getting some professional support can help.

Brain fog and fatigue are your nervous system’s way of asking for recovery time, so supporting your body can make the fog lift faster. Start with water or an electrolyte drink, followed by a small, balanced meal or snack. Light movement like walking or stretching also helps by boosting circulation and clearing leftover stress hormones, while short breaks from screens give your brain a reset.

Some people find that changing environments—stepping outside for fresh air, moving to a quieter space, or dimming harsh lighting—makes a noticeable difference in clarity. Rest is important, too, but you don’t want to overdo it. A short nap capped at 20–30 minutes usually helps more than staying in bed for hours.

The exhaustion you feel after a panic attack is the crash that comes after an adrenaline surge. Basically, when you panic, your body burns through enormous amounts of energy in a short time. Your heart rate rises, your muscles tense, and your brain goes into overdrive to scan for danger.

Even though there isn’t an actual threat, your body doesn’t know that, so it uses up its resources as if there is. Once the panic attack passes, your hormones shift, and your body needs to come down from the emotional intensity. While it’s easy to look at this exhaustion as weakness, it’s really just your body’s way of recovering from an all-systems-on alert. That’s why gentleness is key for recovery.

In a recent development, you can’t always prevent panic attacks, but you can definitely soften the after-effects. The most helpful strategies are proactive, or preventing one before it comes on. Think: getting consistent sleep, eating balanced meals to keep blood sugar steady, staying hydrated, and limiting alcohol or excessive caffeine.

Recent findings suggest that some people find it useful to have a short aftercare routine ready, too, such as hydrating, stretching, or texting a friend once the panic subsides. This helps to prevent the hangover from stretching out longer than necessary.

It has been revealed that over time, therapy and skills training can also reduce both the frequency of panic attacks and the severity of hangovers. You’ll essentially learn how to give your nervous system a softer landing.

Industry observers note that headaches and sore muscles are common after a panic attack. During panic, your jaw, neck, shoulders, and chest may tighten without you noticing, and fast, shallow breathing could add to the headache.

Unclenching your jaw, rolling your shoulders, or holding a cool compress to your forehead may help. Get care right away if you have a sudden, severe headache, chest pain, numbness or weakness, trouble speaking, or vision changes. If your headache lasts longer than you’d expect, check in with your doctor or primary care provider.

Recent findings suggest that after a panic attack, give your body a few minutes to settle before you do anything else. Stay where you are if it’s safe, and take a few slow breaths with a longer exhale.

In a recent development, shakiness or fog is a normal part of coming down from panic, so you don’t need to push through it. Once the first wave passes, tell someone you trust what happened and lower the demands on yourself for the rest of the day. The 12 tips above have ideas for the hours that follow. If panic attacks keep happening, talking with a doctor or mental health professional may help.

Tech Report: Study: Menstrual Cycle Irregularities Linked to ADHD, Depression, Anxiety in Girls

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1034 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Menstrual cycle irregularities, like severe menstrual pain and premenstrual symptoms, are associated with mental health conditions in adolescent girls, according to a latest study.
  • Several menstrual cycle characteristics, including timing of menarche, cycle regularity, menstrual pain, and severity of premenstrual symptoms, are associated with more common and severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and ADHD in adolescent girls, according to a recent study published in European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry.1.
  • The longitudinal study followed 5,673 adolescent girls, ages 9 to 11, over a seven-year period, with annual assessments up to ages 14 to 17.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Menstrual cycle irregularities, like severe menstrual pain and premenstrual symptoms, are associated with mental health conditions in adolescent girls, according to a latest study.

Several menstrual cycle characteristics, including timing of menarche, cycle regularity, menstrual pain, and severity of premenstrual symptoms, are associated with more common and severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and ADHD in adolescent girls, according to a recent study published in European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry.1.

The longitudinal study followed 5,673 adolescent girls, ages 9 to 11, over a seven-year period, with annual assessments up to ages 14 to 17.

According to recent reports, study participants self-reported the severity of premenstrual symptoms, such as irritability and fatigue, and the intensity of period pain (categorized as mild, moderate, or severe). Findings indicated that severe menstrual pain was associated with higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptoms.

In a recent development, premenstrual symptoms demonstrated a graded pattern in their association with mental health outcomes. Mild premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety symptom scores. Moderate premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety and depression symptom scores. Severe premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptom scores.

The researchers offered several social and biological factors as potential explanations for these results.

“Psychosocially, menstrual pain and [premenstrual symptoms] may result in functional impairment – including missed school, disrupted sleep, reduced social participation – which may contribute to emotional distress,” they wrote.

Sources indicate that the study explained that intense period pain and premenstrual distress may activate inflammatory and pain-sensitivity pathways, increasing vulnerability to anxiety and depression. Researchers also noted that the neurobiological mechanisms for processing pain may overlap with those involved in attention and focus, which could help explain the connection between menstrual pain and ADHD symptoms.

In a recent development, researchers also suggested that fluctuating estrogen and progesterone may help to explain the connection between severe premenstrual symptoms and higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptom scores. These hormones heavily affect serotonin, dopamine, and GABA in the brain. Serotonin is linked to mood; dopamine controls motivation and reward processing; and GABA is crucial for emotional processing and regulation. When hormones fluctuate before a menstrual cycle, these neurotransmitters are impacted too, which, in turn, may influence symptoms of anxiety, depression, and ADHD.

It has been revealed that the relationship between ADHD and hormonal fluctuations is a pressing subject for many ADDitude readers with lived experience. In an ADDitude survey of nearly 2,000 women with ADHD, almost one in two respondents noted that hormonal fluctuations had a “life-altering” or “severe” impact on their ADHD.

“I know that the week before my period I am a complete mess,” Addison, an ADDitude reader, said. “I have to prepare for the fact that my world feels like it’s falling apart emotionally, and I hate the way that I look the most that week. These are weeks I often avoid being with people, as I know I am not the most positive and am the most sensitive.”.

“I used to have lots of irritability, food cravings, tiredness, and was fuzzy-headed three to four days before my period started,” said Connie, another reader.

“I suffer from symptoms like uncontrolled fits of anger and crying spells and feeling extremely overwhelmed the days before my period. I’m even more moody, irritable and have more trouble concentrating,” said ADDitude reader Elena.

Moreover, women with ADHD are disproportionately affected by premenstrual disorders with more than 40% of women with ADHD experiencing premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) compared to 3% to 9% of women overall.2, 3 PMDD is also heavily tied to hormonal shifts and mental health.

“PMDD is caused by a high sensitivity to fluctuations in estrogen and progesterone, as well as decreases in serotonin – hormonal changes that happen during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle,” wrote Dara Abraham, D.O. in an ADDitude article. “During the luteal phase that follows ovulation, estrogen decreases, as do dopamine, serotonin, and eventually progesterone. These changes cause painful and distressing symptoms until the menstruation begins and hormone levels rise again.”.

The study also found that irregular menstrual cycles were linked to higher depression and anxiety symptom scores. The longer a girl had been having her menstrual cycles, the stronger the link between irregular periods and depression and anxiety symptoms became. Likewise, earlier age at menarche was associated with higher depression symptom scores.

While the study focused specifically on early age at menarche, previous research suggests that early puberty more broadly may have an association to ADHD.

Sources indicate that “Researchers are examining why girls with ADHD have about twice the risk for early puberty, and why autistic girls are up to four times more likely to experience early puberty compared to other children,” wrote Molly Nikolas, Ph.D. in an ADDitude article. “In addition to higher rates of obesity and social stress, which could accelerate the onset of puberty, neurodivergent girls may experience differences in dopamine activity, stress response, and immune and neuroendocrine systems — all of which may affect sexual development.”.

According to recent reports, the researchers listed several limitations to the study. Menstrual cycle characteristics were gathered through an annual self-report, and parents reported mental health symptoms. In addition, the relationship between menstrual characteristics and mental health symptoms may be bidirectional. The researchers also reported the associations were modest and that future studies are needed to further explore the potential social and biological mechanisms involved.

The study’s authors said they hope their findings will help healthcare professionals consider menstrual cycle characteristics as potentially meaningful insight when evaluating the mental health of adolescent girls.

1 Marla, S., Gangaraju, S.H., Nguyen, J. et al. Association between menstrual cycle characteristics and mental health in early adolescence. Eur Child Adolesc Psychiatry 35, 4035–4049 (2026). https://doi.org/10.1007/s00787-026-03163-8.

2 Team, A. E. (2025). PMDD and ADHD: Understanding the connection and managing symptoms. ADDA – Attention Deficit Disorder Association. https://add.org/pmdd-and-adhd/.

3 Pooja Thakrar, Kalyani Bhukar, Rajat Oswal, Premenstrual dysphoric disorder: Prevalence, quality of life and disability due to illness among medical and paramedical students.
